notice: Human items are US public domain (all published before 1929). AI items were generated for this project and store the verbatim prompt. No item is scraped, no item is in copyright, and no AI detector is used to decide any answer. Categories are deliberately orthogonal to the answer: every category contains both human and AI items, so the category label can never be used to guess.

tells.name: Generic phrasing
tells.explanation: Language that could describe almost anything. Concrete, oddly specific detail is a human fingerprint.

tells.name: The tidy bow
tells.explanation: A closing sentence that summarises the feeling instead of ending on the next small fact.

tells.name: Uniform rhythm
tells.explanation: Sentences of suspiciously even length and shape. Human prose lurches; it runs long, then stops short.

tells.name: Hedged emotion
tells.explanation: Feelings held at arm's length — 'somewhat', 'a sense of', 'to some degree' — rather than stated plainly or shown in action.

tells.name: Abstraction stack
tells.explanation: Piles of abstract nouns doing work a concrete image should be doing.

tells.name: Safe consensus
tells.explanation: Everyone agrees, nothing is at stake, and no one holds an inconvenient opinion.

tells.name: Unbudgeted detail
tells.explanation: A detail too strange or too useless to have been invented for effect. Real observation keeps things it does not need.

tells.name: Awkward on purpose
tells.explanation: Period grammar, comma-spliced clauses and constructions a fluency-optimised model would quietly smooth away.

tells.name: Ragged rhythm
tells.explanation: A sentence that changes direction mid-flight, or lengths that lurch from sixty words to four.

tells.name: Sometimes there is no tell
tells.explanation: Some items give nothing away. A clean, balanced sentence is not evidence of a machine. The answer comes from provenance, never from a feeling — and knowing when you are guessing is part of the skill.

items.label: ai
items.body: The lighthouse had stood on the point for ninety years, and in all that time it had never once failed to burn. Old Tomas climbed its stairs each evening as his father had, and his father before him, carrying the small brass can of oil. The sea was cruel and the winters were long, but the light endured. In the end, it was not the lamp that guided the ships home, but the faith of the man who tended it.
items.explanation: The last sentence steps outside the story to explain what the story meant. Human fiction usually ends on the next concrete thing — the oil can, the stairs — and trusts you to draw the moral yourself.

provenance.prompt: Write a four-sentence opening for a literary novel about a lighthouse keeper. End with a summarising line about faith.

review.note: Unambiguous: the closing aphorism is a generated flourish, and the passage belongs to no published work.

items.label: human
items.body: It is a truth universally acknowledged, that a single man in possession of a good fortune, must be in want of a wife.
items.explanation: The comma before 'that' is period punctuation no modern editor would leave in place, and the mock-legal cadence — 'universally acknowledged', 'in possession of', 'in want of' — is a joke at its own expense: it announces a truth it intends to demolish.

review.note: Unambiguous: verbatim from a work published in 1813.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: human
items.body: Alice was beginning to get very tired of sitting by her sister on the bank, and of having nothing to do: once or twice she had peeped into the book her sister was reading, but it had no pictures or conversations in it, "and what is the use of a book," thought Alice, "without pictures or conversations?"
items.explanation: One sentence that runs sixty words, changes direction twice at a colon, and finishes inside a quoted thought. A model asked for an opening paragraph almost always delivers three tidy sentences instead.

review.note: Unambiguous: verbatim from a work published in 1865.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: ai
items.body: 14 October. The rain returned this morning and stayed through the afternoon. I walked to the post office and found no letter waiting for me. The garden is finished for the year and the beds look bare. I have begun reading in the evenings, which helps to pass the time.
items.explanation: Four sentences of almost identical length, each a clean independent clause with one balancing phrase attached. Real diaries abbreviate, break off, and skip the connective tissue — nobody writing for themselves is this evenly paced.

provenance.prompt: Write a five-line diary entry for a quiet autumn day in a rural household, early twentieth century, plain and undramatic.

review.note: Unambiguous by provenance; the even pacing is the intended tell.

items.label: ai
items.body: There was in her manner a quality of restraint that suggested both dignity and sorrow, as though grief had been folded carefully and put away in a drawer she no longer opened. The house behind her held the silence of long habit. Whatever loss had occurred there had long since settled into the architecture of daily life, becoming less an event than a condition.
items.explanation: 'A quality of restraint', 'the silence of long habit', 'the architecture of daily life' — three abstractions doing the work one concrete image would do better. The drawer is the only real object in the passage, and it is a simile rather than a thing in the room.

items.label: human
items.body: The Nellie, a cruising yawl, swung to her anchor without a flutter of the sails, and was at rest.
items.explanation: 'A cruising yawl' and 'swung to her anchor' are unbudgeted: the rig of the boat does nothing for the story, and only someone who knew boats would spend words on it. Generated prose tends to say 'a small sailing boat' because that is what the sentence actually needs.

review.note: Unambiguous: verbatim from a work published in 1899.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: ai
items.body: He did not think of her often, and when he did it was without bitterness, only a faint sense of something misplaced, the way a man might notice the absence of a coat he had not worn in years. The road out of town was long and the evening was coming on. He walked it as he had walked it before, and found that he minded less than he had expected to.
items.explanation: Every feeling is kept at a safe distance: 'without bitterness', 'a faint sense of something misplaced', 'minded less than he had expected'. Nothing is ever simply felt. This one is genuinely hard — the restraint reads as craft until you notice it never once commits.

provenance.prompt: Write three sentences of understated literary fiction: a man leaving a town, thinking about a woman he no longer loves. Restrained, no melodrama.

review.note: Hard but not unfair: the answer is decided by provenance, and the hedging pattern is a real, teachable signal.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: human
items.body: It was the best of times, it was the worst of times, it was the age of wisdom, it was the age of foolishness, it was the epoch of belief, it was the epoch of incredulity, it was the season of Light, it was the season of Darkness, it was the spring of hope, it was the winter of despair.
items.explanation: Ten independent clauses strung together on commas — a comma splice, repeated nine times on purpose. Asked for an opening line, a model breaks this into three sentences and loses the whole effect.

review.note: Unambiguous: verbatim from a work published in 1859.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: ai
items.body: 3 March. A difficult week at the mill, though I am trying to keep my spirits up. The men have been patient with me and I am grateful for it. Mr. Hale says the orders will come again in the spring and I believe he is right. If nothing else, this winter has taught me the value of steady work and good company.
items.explanation: A private diary does not close the week with a lesson learned. The last sentence is written for a reader — and a diary has none.

provenance.prompt: Write a short diary entry from a mill supervisor during a slow winter, hopeful in tone, ending on a reflection.

review.note: Unambiguous by provenance; the closing moral is the intended tell.

items.label: human
items.body: You will rejoice to hear that no disaster has accompanied the commencement of an enterprise which you have regarded with such evil forebodings.
items.explanation: This one is a trap for the tell you just learned: 'the commencement of an enterprise' is exactly the abstraction stack that usually flags a machine. What saves it is 'evil forebodings' — a collocation that died around 1850 and that no fluency-optimised model reaches for.

review.note: Unambiguous: verbatim from a work published in 1818. Deliberately placed to show that a tell is contextual, not proof.

items.body: The train arrived at noon and the passengers stepped down onto the platform. The porters took the trunks and carried them toward the station house. A woman in grey stood apart from the others and watched the road. The sky was pale and the wind moved through the empty field beyond.
items.explanation: Four sentences, near-identical length, every one built the same way: subject, verb, object, and a second clause joined with 'and'. Human paragraphs vary the machinery; this one never does.

items.body: 9 June. I find that I am somewhat unsettled by the news from home, though I would not call it distress exactly. There is a sense of distance that has grown between us which I do not fully understand. I intend to write to her, and expect that doing so will help to some degree.
items.explanation: 'Somewhat unsettled', 'would not call it distress exactly', 'to some degree'. People hedge in letters they expect others to read; in a private entry they usually just say the thing.

items.body: All happy families are alike; each unhappy family is unhappy in its own way.
items.explanation: There is no tell here, and you should distrust anyone who claims to see one. It is clean, balanced and modern-sounding — exactly what a good model produces. items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: ai
items.body: The city in those years was a place of great energy and great poverty, where fortunes were made in a season and lost in an afternoon. Men came from everywhere, carrying whatever they had, and the streets were loud from morning until well past dark. It was, everyone agreed, a remarkable time to be alive.
items.explanation: Not one street is named, not one price quoted, not one person. Swap 'the city' for any boomtown in any century and nothing breaks — which is precisely what a passage assembled from the average of all such passages looks like.

provenance.prompt: Write three sentences evoking a booming nineteenth-century city, in the voice of a retrospective narrator.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: human
items.body: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago—never mind how long precisely—having little or no money in my purse, and nothing particular to interest me on shore, I thought I would sail about a little and see the watery part of the world.
items.explanation: Three words, then a sixty-word sentence that interrupts itself with an em-dash aside and refuses to say how long ago. The refusal is the human part: a model asked for an opening supplies the number.

review.note: Unambiguous: verbatim from a work published in 1851.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: ai
items.body: Marta had kept the bakery on the corner for thirty-one years, and every morning she was there before the light. Her hands knew the dough the way other hands know a face. Customers came and went, children grew and moved away, and still the ovens were lit at four. Some people, she thought, are simply made of the work they do.
items.explanation: 'Thirty-one years' and 'lit at four' are good, concrete details — and then the last line throws them away to state the theme outright. The tidy bow is the tell, not the details before it.

provenance.prompt: Write four warm sentences about an elderly baker who has run the same shop for decades, ending on a reflective line.

items.label: human
items.body: It is very seldom that mere ordinary people like John and myself secure ancestral halls for the summer.
items.explanation: 'John and myself' is a grammatical slip a fluency-optimised model corrects to 'John and I' without being asked. Here it is left in, because it characterises the narrator — and the flat 'mere ordinary people' next to 'ancestral halls' is doing quiet, unexplained irony.

items.body: 3 May. Bistritz.—Left Munich at 8:35 P.M., on 1st May, arriving at Vienna early next morning; should have arrived at 6:46, but train was an hour late.
items.explanation: 8:35, 6:46, an hour late. Nobody invents a timetable this precise for atmosphere — and note the dropped articles ('but train was an hour late'), the shorthand of someone writing fast for themselves.

items.altText: A short personal journal or letter entry.

items.label: ai
items.body: Opinion in the village was divided, though not sharply, and most agreed that the matter would resolve itself in time. The elder Brennan said as much at the meeting, and no one contradicted him. It was generally felt that patience was the wiser course, and that whatever had happened at the mill was best left to those who understood it.
items.explanation: A village where opinion is 'divided, though not sharply' and 'no one contradicted him' is a village with nothing at stake. Real accounts of a divided village name the person who would not let it go.

items.altText: A short passage of prose fiction.

items.label: ai
items.body: 22 November. The days grow shorter and the house is quiet. I have been thinking a great deal lately about the passage of time and the way ordinary things acquire meaning only after they are gone. There is a comfort in routine that I did not appreciate when I was younger. Tomorrow I shall try to rise earlier.
items.explanation: Nothing here belongs to one life. No name, no price, no specific irritation, no weather beyond 'the days grow shorter'. Compare the 8:35 train two rounds ago: that is what a real diary spends its words on.

provenance.prompt: Write a reflective diary entry for a late November evening, contemplative, about time and routine.

review.note: Hard but fair: the absence of any specific anchor is a real and teachable signal.
